title: Focal Length Explained: mm, Crop Factor and Phone Zoom — cv.cm
description: Focal length explained: what mm means, wide to telephoto angles of view, crop factor and phone 0.5x to 5x lenses, why faces distort, and the best portrait lengths.
h1: What does focal length mean and which one should you use?
answer: Focal length, in millimetres, sets how much of the scene a lens shows. A short focal length such as 16 to 35 mm is wide and shows a lot; 50 mm is close to a natural view; 85 mm and longer is telephoto and magnifies distant subjects. The number is the lens's real focal length; on smaller sensors and phones, compare by the full-frame equivalent.

body: Focal length is an optical distance, not the physical length of the lens. It is the distance from the lens's optical centre to the sensor when the lens is focused at infinity. A longer focal length projects a larger image of the same scene, so the sensor sees a narrower slice of it: the angle of view gets smaller and distant things look bigger.
Doubling the focal length halves the width of the scene and makes everything in it twice as large in the frame. A 100 mm lens shows a subject twice as large as a 50 mm lens from the same spot.

body: A zoom lens covers a range, such as 24-70 mm. A prime lens has one focal length, such as 50 mm; primes are usually smaller, brighter (lower f-number) and cheaper for their quality, but you move your feet to change framing.

Lens focal lengths are usually compared on a full-frame sensor, 36 by 24 mm, the size of 35 mm film. Smaller sensors record only the centre of the lens's image, which looks like a crop, so the same lens gives a narrower view. The crop factor tells you by how much.

body: The lens itself does not change. A 50 mm lens is 50 mm on any camera; only the angle of view changes. Equivalence is a way to compare framing. Depth of field and noise also shift with sensor size, but that is covered in the aperture and ISO articles.

Phone lenses have very short real focal lengths, a few millimetres, on small sensors. Phone makers therefore describe them as zoom steps relative to the main camera, or as full-frame equivalents. The exact numbers vary by model, but these are typical:

body: Use the buttons, not pinching, when you can. Pinching between steps often uses digital zoom, which crops and enlarges the image and loses detail. In dim light, the 1x main camera usually gives the cleanest result, because it has the largest sensor and brightest lens.
Rule of thumb: for people, step back and use 2x or 3x instead of standing close at 1x or 0.5x.

sections.h: Perspective and face distortion: it is the distance, not the lens
body: Wide-angle selfies make noses look big and ears small. Telephoto portraits look flatter. The lens is not causing this directly. Perspective depends only on the distance between the camera and the subject. The lens choice decides how far you stand to get the framing you want.
Consider a head-and-shoulders portrait on full frame. To fill the frame, you stand roughly:

ul: 24 mm: about 35 cm from the face. The ears are about 10 cm farther away than the nose, so the nose looks about 30 percent larger relative to them. Faces look rounder and the nose prominent.
50 mm: about 70 cm. Still slightly enlarged features if very tight.
85 mm: about 1.2 m. The nose is enlarged by under 10 percent. Faces look natural and flattering to most people.
135 mm: about 1.9 m. Faces look slightly flatter; backgrounds look closer and larger.

body: You can test this yourself: take one photo at 24 mm from 35 cm, then a second at 24 mm from 1.2 m and crop it to the same framing. The cropped photo shows the same face shape as an 85 mm photo from 1.2 m, only with less detail. This is also why selfies at arm length look different from photos taken by a friend.

Distance changes the background too. With a long lens from far away, the background appears larger and closer behind the subject, often called compression. With a wide lens from close up, the background looks small and far away. Use this deliberately: a long lens can fill the frame behind a person with a single tree or a mountain; a wide lens shows the whole place.
Wide-angle lenses also stretch objects near the edges of the frame. Keep faces and bodies near the centre of a wide shot, and hold the camera level to avoid buildings leaning backwards.

body: 50 mm is a good first lens: affordable, bright, and versatile from half body to full body. 85 mm is the classic head-and-shoulders lens because it puts you at about 1 to 2 m, a comfortable talking distance, with natural features. 135 mm gives even smoother backgrounds but needs more space, which is hard indoors.
To compare them on the same sitter without buying anything, cv.cm's portrait camera simulator has 24, 35, 50, 85 and 135 mm lenses plus a phone lens and a subject distance control.

sections.h: Choosing a focal length: a quick checklist

ol: Decide the framing: whole scene, full body, half body or face.
Decide the distance you can or want to stand at: a small room limits you to wide lenses; a stage limits you to long ones.
For people, choose the longest focal length that still lets you stand where you need to.
For places, start at 24 to 35 mm. Only go wider when you cannot step back.
Check the shutter speed: longer lenses show more hand shake, so use about 1 divided by the equivalent focal length or faster.
On a phone, use the lens buttons instead of pinching, and use 1x in low light.

ul: Big nose in a selfie or close portrait: step back and use 2x or a longer lens.
Legs look short in a full-body shot: do not stand very close with a wide lens pointing down. Step back, lower the camera to about waist height and use 50 mm or 2x.
People at the edge of a group look stretched: keep them nearer the centre or use a longer lens from farther away.
Telephoto photos are blurred: hand shake is magnified. Use a faster shutter or a support.
Zoomed phone photo looks smeared: you went past the optical steps into digital zoom. Use the nearest lens button and crop later.

faq.q: Is 50 mm or 85 mm better for portraits?
faq.a: 85 mm gives more flattering faces for head-and-shoulders shots and more background blur. 50 mm is more versatile, works in smaller rooms and suits half-body and full-body portraits.

faq.q: What focal length is closest to the human eye?
faq.a: About 40 to 50 mm on full frame gives a perspective and size similar to normal vision, which is why 50 mm is called a normal lens. Our total field of view is much wider.

faq.q: Does a crop sensor make my lens longer?
faq.a: No. The focal length stays the same, but the smaller sensor records a narrower angle of view. A 50 mm lens on a 1.5x APS-C camera frames like a 75 mm lens on full frame.

faq.q: What mm is the iPhone or Android main camera?
faq.a: Most phone main cameras are equivalent to about 23 to 26 mm on full frame. The real focal length is only a few millimetres because the sensor is small.

faq.q: Why do wide-angle photos make people look distorted?
faq.a: With a wide lens you usually stand very close, which enlarges nearby features. Wide lenses also stretch objects near the frame edges. Step back and use a longer focal length.
